title: Waves
tagline: Transverse and longitudinal waves, progressive waves, displacement relation, speed, principle of superposition, reflection, beats and the Doppler effect.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ISC Class XI Physics syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Syllabus unit and chapter title were taken from the official-verified ISC Physics registry entry; no board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: A wave is a disturbance that travels through a medium or through space, carrying energy without carrying matter along with it. In this chapter we describe waves in their simplest forms. We begin by distinguishing transverse and longitudinal waves, then move to the description of a progressive wave by its displacement relation. After that we study wave speed, the principle of superposition, reflection at a boundary, the phenomenon of beats when two waves are nearly equal in frequency, and the Doppler effect, which explains why a moving source changes the observed frequency.

facts.label: Core ideas
facts.value: Transverse and longitudinal waves; progressive wave equation; wave speed; superposition; reflection; standing waves and normal modes; beats; Doppler effect

learningOutcomes: Write and interpret a simple progressive wave equation.
Relate wave speed to wavelength and frequency.
Explain reflection of waves at a boundary.
Explain beats and how they arise.
Explain the Doppler effect in simple cases.

blocks.text: Waves can be classified by the direction of particle motion compared with the direction of wave travel. In a transverse wave, the particles move perpendicular to the direction of propagation, as in a wave on a string. In a longitudinal wave, the particles move parallel to the direction of propagation, as in sound waves in air. Both types transfer energy, but they do so in different ways.

items: Transverse wave: particle motion is perpendicular to wave direction.
Longitudinal wave: particle motion is parallel to wave direction.
Both transfer energy, not matter.
Sound in air is a longitudinal wave.

items.text: If a rope is moved up and down, the wave travels along the rope while each point on the rope moves up and down. That is a transverse wave.
items.note: The motion of the particles is not the same as the motion of the wave itself.

blocks.text: A simple progressive wave can be described by a displacement relation of the form y = A sin(kx - omega t) or a similar form, depending on the choice of origin and direction. In such a relation, A is the amplitude, k is the propagation constant, and omega is the angular frequency. The wave travels with a speed related to wavelength and frequency. From the displacement relation, one can find the shape of the wave and how it moves in time.

items: A progressive wave travels through the medium.
Amplitude is the maximum displacement.
k relates to wavelength; omega relates to frequency.
Wave speed is related to wavelength and frequency.

items.text: If the wavelength is doubled while the frequency is held fixed, the wave speed must also double, because speed = wavelength x frequency.
items.note: This relation is one of the simplest and most useful in wave motion.

blocks.text: The speed of a wave depends on the medium. For a wave on a string, the speed depends on the tension and the linear density. For sound waves, the speed depends on the properties of the medium, such as its elasticity and density. The general idea is that the wave speed is a property of the medium, while the frequency and wavelength are linked by that speed. If the frequency changes, the wavelength changes so that the product still equals the speed.

items: Wave speed depends on the medium.
For a stretched string, speed depends on tension and linear density.
Speed = wavelength x frequency.
Changing frequency changes wavelength if the speed is fixed.

items.text: If a wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 2 m, its speed is 50 x 2 = 100 m/s.
items.note: This relation lets one quantity be found from the other two.

blocks.text: When two or more waves travel through the same region, the resultant displacement at any point is the sum of the displacements due to each wave. This is the principle of superposition. It explains interference, beats and the formation of standing waves. The principle holds for waves that are not too large in amplitude in most simple situations.

items: Resultant displacement is the sum of individual displacements.
It explains interference and beats.
It is also the basis for standing waves.
It applies to linear wave motion.

items.text: If two pulses travelling in opposite directions meet, the displacement at that moment is the sum of the two pulse displacements.
items.note: The waves do not bounce off each other permanently; they pass through and the resultant is the instantaneous sum.

blocks.text: When a wave meets a boundary, it is partly or wholly reflected. The nature of the reflection depends on the boundary. Beats occur when two waves of slightly different frequencies superpose. The sound gets alternately loud and soft because the waves go in and out of phase. The beat frequency is the difference between the two frequencies. This is a practical way to tune instruments and to compare frequencies.

items: Waves can be reflected at boundaries.
Beats arise from superposition of nearly equal frequencies.
Beat frequency equals the difference of the frequencies.
Beats are heard as a periodic rise and fall in loudness.

items.text: If two sounds have frequencies 256 Hz and 260 Hz, the beat frequency is 4 Hz, so the loudness varies four times per second.
items.note: The beats are not because one frequency is bigger, but because the two combine periodically.

blocks.text: The Doppler effect is the change in observed frequency when the source and observer are moving relative to each other. If the source approaches, the observed frequency is higher; if it moves away, the observed frequency is lower. The effect is common with sound, such as a vehicle passing by, and it also occurs with light, where it is used in astronomy. In simple cases, the change depends on the relative motion.

items: Observed frequency changes with relative motion.
Apparent frequency is higher when the source approaches.
Apparent frequency is lower when the source moves away.
The effect occurs for sound and light.

items.text: The pitch of a siren sounds higher as an ambulance approaches and lower as it passes and moves away. That change is the Doppler effect.
items.note: It is relative motion, not speed alone, that matters for the shift.

keyPoints: Transverse waves have particle motion perpendicular to propagation; longitudinal waves have it parallel.
A progressive wave can be described by a displacement relation with amplitude, wavelength and frequency.
Wave speed equals wavelength times frequency.
The principle of superposition says displacements add.
Beats arise from two nearly equal frequencies; beat frequency is their difference.
The Doppler effect changes perceived frequency due to relative motion.
examFocus: When using speed = wavelength x frequency, keep units consistent for wavelength and frequency.
For beats, the beat frequency is the difference of the frequencies, not their sum.

vocabulary.meaning: A disturbance that travels and transfers energy without transferring matter.
A wave in which particle motion is perpendicular to the direction of propagation.
A wave in which particle motion is parallel to the direction of propagation.
The maximum displacement of a wave from its equilibrium position.
The principle that displacements add when waves overlap.
The periodic variation in amplitude produced by two nearly equal frequencies.

questions.explanation: Sound in air is a longitudinal wave because particle motion is parallel to propagation.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking all waves in daily life are transverse.

questions.prompt: If the wavelength is 2 m and the frequency is 50 Hz, the wave speed is:
questions.explanation: Speed = wavelength x frequency = 2 x 50 = 100 m/s.
questions.commonMistake: Dividing instead of multiplying, or swapping wavelength and frequency.

questions.prompt: What is the principle of superposition?
questions.answer: It states that when two or more waves overlap, the resultant displacement at a point is the sum of the individual displacements.
questions.explanation: This principle explains interference, beats and standing waves.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the waves cancel permanently or that they cannot overlap.

questions.prompt: Two sounds of frequencies 256 Hz and 260 Hz are heard together. What is the beat frequency?
questions.commonMistake: Adding the frequencies, or confusing beat frequency with either frequency alone.

questions.prompt: A source of sound approaches a stationary observer. What happens to the observed frequency, and why?
questions.answer: The observed frequency increases because the waves are received more frequently when the source moves toward the observer, so the apparent pitch rises.
questions.explanation: This is the Doppler effect; the change is due to relative motion between source and observer.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the source’s own frequency changes, rather than the apparent frequency observed.
